app.name: VAM
mixer.noChannels: No strips yet. Add one to begin.
strip.name: Name
send.lockedWhy: This channel is the far end of this bus. Sending it back to itself is what makes an echo, so the engine works it out from the pairing and does not offer it as a choice.
automix.title: Automix
automix.sub: Gain sharing across the microphones that take part. What it takes away it gives back somewhere else, so the room stays as loud as it was.
recording.title: Recording
diag.title: Diagnostics
settings.title: Settings
settings.addressWhy: The engine on this machine is used unless you name another one. A bare name or address is completed for you.
settings.notAnAddress: That is not an address this console can use.
settings.noEngineHere: This console cannot start an engine. Start one on the computer with the microphones, and name it above.
settings.startFailed: No engine was running and one could not be started here.
settings.startedButSilent: An engine was started here but never answered. Its own log will say why.
settings.stopEngineConfirm: Stop the engine? Sound stops, and any recording is closed.
settings.engineLifeWhy: The engine keeps running when this window is closed, so a meeting is not ended by closing a console. Stopping it here is how you end one on purpose.
close.title: Close VAM?
close.sub: The engine is a separate program. It keeps running unless you say otherwise, so that closing a console cannot end a meeting.
close.stopEngine.sub: Sound stops and any recording is closed properly.
close.leaveRunning.sub: The mix carries on. Open VAM again to get back to it.
monitors.sub: What each pair of headphones hears. Changing it never touches what goes out.
channel.removeWhy: Remove {0}? Its sends go with it, and the recording keeps the track it has already written.
chain.head: Input · trim, polarity, mono
chain.alwaysFirst: Always first in the chain. The settings below are editable.
chain.alwaysLast: Always last in the chain. The settings below are editable.
chain.anchoredWhy: Fixed position — this link cannot be dragged.
chain.vadTap: Voice activity is read here, before the denoise — because denoise removes what the detector keys on.
chain.mandatory: Added by the engine. A stream bus always ends in a limiter.
chain.mandatoryWhy: The engine put this here and will not let it be removed.
send.preWhy: Monitor sends are pre-fader, so moving a fader does not change what the person in the chair hears.
help.engine: The engine runs headless. Closing this window does not stop the meeting.
help.dropouts: Buffer underruns and overruns since the engine started. This number must stay at zero.
help.load: How much of the callback deadline the worst recent block used. Above 70% the callback starts missing it.
help.headroom: What is left of the callback deadline. This is the one that runs out.
help.automixSwitch: Global automix bypass. One click from any view, and amber while it is off so nobody forgets.
help.rate: The rate the device claims, beside the rate it is actually running at.
help.share: How much of the automixer gain this channel is holding, between the depth floor and 0 dB.
help.threshold: Where the gate opens. A voice below this line is not reaching the mix.
help.mute: Mute. The strip goes grey so it reads as off from across the room.
help.solo: Solo — pre-fade listen into the monitor buses. It never touches what goes out.
help.monoFold: Sums a stereo device to one channel. Almost every conference microphone wants this — a stereo image is meaningless for a single voice and doubles the work downstream.
help.limiter: Brick-wall limiter activity. On a stream bus it is not optional, because a stream that clips cannot be repaired afterwards.
help.reorder: Drag a strip by its grip to reorder. Off by default, because a fader and a strip are the same gesture on a touchscreen.
help.density: Fit more strips on screen — meters and mutes only.
help.addInput: Add an input strip. The device list comes from the engine machine.
help.head: Trim, polarity and mono fold describe the signal arriving rather than a treatment of it, so they cannot be dragged further down the chain.
help.tail: The automix gain is applied after the fader, so the operator fader keeps meaning what it says.
help.trim: Digital gain before anything else, ±24 dB. Set it so the meter sits around −18 dBFS when someone speaks normally — everything downstream assumes a sane input level.
help.polarity: Flips the waveform. It matters when two microphones pick up the same speaker: out of phase they cancel and the voice goes thin and hollow. Flip one and listen — if it suddenly gets fuller, leave it flipped.
help.participate: Channels that are not competing for the same room should stay out. The audience microphone and the online feed are out by default, because sharing gain with a loudspeaker playing back what the mix just sent is a slow feedback loop.
help.weight: Biases the sharing for a microphone that is quieter or further away by nature. A higher weight makes this channel win ties.
help.mod.vam.gain: Plain gain, applied before everything after it. Use trim for setting the input level and this for shaping what the chain sees.
help.mod.vam.highpass: Removes what is below a voice — footsteps, table knocks, air handling. 80 Hz is safe for speech; raise it until the room noise goes and stop before the voice thins.
help.mod.vam.gate: Silences a microphone that nobody is speaking into. Set the threshold just above the room noise: if a quiet voice disappears, it is too high.
help.mod.vam.compressor: Evens out the difference between somebody leaning in and somebody sitting back. Start at a ratio of 3 and lower the threshold until the loud parts move a few decibels.
help.mod.vam.equaliser: Four bands plus shelves. Cutting is safer than boosting — a cut around 300 Hz clears a boxy room, and a small lift near 3 kHz helps consonants carry.
help.mod.vam.limiter: A ceiling nothing gets past. It is the last thing in the path, and on a stream bus it is not optional.
help.mod.vam.adaptivegain: Holds a speaker at a steady level as they move around. Slower than a compressor and meant for the whole meeting rather than for one sentence.
help.mod.vam.denoise: Takes out steady background noise — ventilation, a projector fan. It cannot help with another voice, and pushed hard it makes speech sound underwater.
bus.nothingExcluded: Nothing is excluded from this bus.
automix.band: Last 30 seconds — who held the gain
automix.bandWhy: This band is how an operator learns to trust the automixer instead of reaching for the faders.
automix.switchLives: The global switch is in the status bar, one click from any view, and it turns amber while it is off so nobody forgets.
help.depth: How far the automixer may turn a channel down. It is a floor, not a gate: a microphone held at the floor is still in the mix, quietly, so somebody interrupting is heard immediately rather than after a gate opens.
help.response: How fast the gain moves between microphones. Too fast and it chatters on a pause; too slow and the first word of an answer is quiet.
monitors.intro: Each headphone feed is a full bus with its own source selection — not a monitor of the master. The same switching is on the bar at the bottom of the mixer, because during setup you change it while you are adjusting everything else.
monitors.busesLater: Feeding a whole bus into a monitor needs bus-to-bus routing, which is phase 1.
monitors.soloWins: A solo on any strip overrides this selection until it is released.
monitors.removeWhy: Remove {0}? Whoever is wearing those headphones stops hearing anything.
diag.sub: Everything worth knowing and not worth looking at during a session. The rule for what lives here rather than on the mixer: if seeing it every day would train you to ignore it, it goes here.
diag.fallbackWhy: No output device is left, so a timer is keeping the graph running. The session survives; nothing that plays sound is clocking it.
diag.allocWhy: The first row is the one that matters. Rule 1 says nothing in the audio path allocates; a test asserts it on a quiet machine and this asserts it on a real one. If it is ever not zero, that is the bug.
diag.dropoutWhy: A list rather than a count, because a hundred dropouts in one bad minute and a hundred spread over three hours have completely different causes.
recording.fixedWhy: Both are on and neither is a choice yet. A recording that could be switched off by accident is a public meeting nobody has a record of.
recording.guardWhy: Recording refuses to start if the disk will not hold the projected session, and says so in the numbers rather than failing later. Silent failure here loses the record of a public meeting.
help.rawInputs: Every input written raw, before the chain and before the automixer. What was said in the room is recoverable whatever the mix did with it on the day.
help.autoStart: The engine starts recording when it starts. Nobody has to remember, which is the point — the meeting nobody recorded is the one where somebody forgot.
recording.sub: Every strip records to its own file, before the fader and before the automixer. What was said in the room is recoverable whatever the mix did with it on the day.
recording.stopWhy: Stop recording? The files are closed and a new recording starts a new folder.
recording.noPicker: This console cannot open a folder picker, and the path belongs to the engine machine rather than to this one. Type it as the engine would see it.
settings.sub: Application-level behaviour. Anything that affects audio lives on the view it belongs to, not here.
settings.startupWhy: Both take effect at the next start rather than now — "load the last console" could not mean anything else. Nobody configures a mixer ten minutes before a session, so the engine comes up in the state it went down in.
help.theme: Deliberately not a choice. A bright screen next to a camera operator in a dim chamber is a problem, and a console that followed a system theme would become one without anybody choosing it.
help.ballistics: Peak rises fast and falls slowly, which is what you want for spotting an overshoot. The average is drawn under it as the body of the bar, because it is what the level sounded like.
help.loadLast: The console an operator spent a meeting setting up is the one that comes back. It is saved on the way out rather than only when somebody asks.
automix.openWhy: Derived from how the gain is actually shared, not from counting microphones over a threshold. Two people each holding half of it reads as two.
help.clip: This channel reached full scale. Click to clear it once you have seen it.
preset.title: Chain preset
preset.deleteWhy: Delete the preset {0}? The chains that came from it keep working — they just stop having somewhere to be restored from.
help.presetModified: The live chain has been changed since this preset was applied.
help.pan: Where the strip sits across a stereo bus. It does nothing to a mono stream, which is what a council watches on a phone speaker — it is for the monitors, where an operator wearing headphones for two hours does not want four microphones stacked in the middle of their head. Constant power, so moving one does not change how loud it is.
bus.removeWhy: Remove {0}? Every send pointing at it goes with it.
help.par.threshold: The level at which this starts working. Set it just above the room noise: if a quiet voice disappears, it is too high, and if a chair scraping gets through, it is too low.
help.par.frequency: Where on the spectrum it acts. Speech lives between about 150 Hz and 4 kHz; below that is the building and above it is hiss.
help.par.gain: How much to add or take away. Cutting is safer than boosting — a boost makes everything at that frequency louder, including the things you did not want.
help.par.q: How wide the band is. Low is broad and gentle, high is narrow and surgical. Start broad; a narrow cut only helps when you already know the exact frequency that is ringing.
help.par.ratio: How hard the compressor pulls once it is working. Three to one is a good starting point for speech; beyond about six it starts to sound squashed.
help.par.attack: How fast it reacts. Too fast and consonants lose their edge; too slow and the loud part is through before anything happens.
help.par.release: How fast it lets go. Too fast and it breathes between words; too slow and one loud sentence turns the next one down.
help.par.strength: How much of the processed signal to use. Rarely worth going to the top — most of the benefit arrives well before that, and the rest costs the voice.
help.par.ceiling: The level nothing gets past. Leave a decibel of room below full scale: a stream that clips cannot be repaired afterwards.
help.par.slope: How steeply it cuts below the frequency. Twelve is gentle and usually enough for desk thumps; twenty-four is for a room with a real rumble problem.
help.par.target: The loudness it aims to hold. Around −18 dBFS leaves headroom for somebody leaning in, which they will.
help.par.hold: How long it stays open after the level drops. Long enough to bridge the pause between words, or it chatters on every breath.
help.par.makeup: Puts back the level the compression took away. Set it so bypassing the compressor does not change how loud the channel sounds.
help.par.knee: How gradually the compression comes in around the threshold. A soft knee is harder to hear working, which is usually what you want for speech.
help.pfl: Puts this strip into the monitors on its own, taken before the fader — so a microphone faded all the way down can still be checked. It reaches the monitors only and never the stream, because an operator checking a microphone should not be broadcasting the check.
